title: Non-Paged Pool Exhaustion
exclusions: Detects three complete five-minute buckets in which the host-level Windows `Memory\Pool Nonpaged Bytes` gauge is at or above an approved exact-host `critical_nonpaged_bytes` policy. It does not discover the Windows pool limit, claim that a fixed byte value is universal, prove actual exhaustion or a leak, identify a pool tag or driver, measure paged pool, equate nonpaged bytes with process memory, or use `Pool Nonpaged Allocs` as outstanding allocations or remaining capacity. `Pool Nonpaged Allocs` is a count of allocation calls regardless of allocation size and is retained only as context. `Available MBytes` is physical-memory context, not the nonpaged-pool denominator. The alert excludes hosts without one enabled, unique, positive policy row and buckets with fewer than four valid samples of all three counters. Missing, stale, localized, duplicated, reset, wrapped, malformed, or multikv-shaped telemetry is source failure rather than a healthy pool. The base SPL applies no notification exception and makes no security, driver culpability, remediation, crash-code, or regulatory-attestation claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `windows_nonpaged_pool_critical_policy` saved-search definition, ACL, fixed time bounds, schedule, dispatch history, and triggered actions; effective `[perfmon://NonpagedPoolCritical]` configuration and `btool` output; add-on, forwarder, Windows, hardware, and search-platform versions; expected-host and source-health results; the reviewed `windows_nonpaged_pool_policy.csv` revision/hash and exact host row; and each alert row containing host, policy identity, critical byte boundary, observation bounds, three qualifying buckets, first/latest/minimum/peak nonpaged bytes and GiB, lowest available MB, first/latest allocation-call values, and allocation-call change when valid. Preserve the corresponding raw events, same-time Performance Monitor or `Get-Counter` samples, Task Manager kernel-memory corroboration where available, PoolMon tag snapshots, driver/change/reboot context, bounded notification exception, incident disposition, and dated positive/negative control outputs. These artifacts show that received measurements crossed the approved policy; they do not prove pool exhaustion, a leak, offending tag/driver, root cause, remediation, or complete fleet coverage. This documentation-only review created no runtime evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated event index with fixed absolute bounds spanning exactly three completed five-minute buckets, ingest one event per minute for each required counter on `host=win-pool-positive`, with `object=Memory`. Set each bucket's `Pool Nonpaged Bytes` samples to 1181116006, 1234803098, and 1288490189 bytes respectively, `Available MBytes=4096`, and monotonically increasing `Pool Nonpaged Allocs`. Provide one unique lookup row with `host=win-pool-positive`, `enabled=1`, `critical_nonpaged_bytes=1073741824`, and `policy_id=lab-1gib`. Expect exactly one result with `complete_buckets=3`, `qualifying_buckets=3`, first/latest values about 1.10/1.20 GiB, and `critical_nonpaged_gib=1`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Run isolated fixed-time variants and expect zero primary rows for each: one of three bucket averages is one byte below policy; only two complete buckets; fewer than four valid samples for any required counter in one bucket; all byte samples negative, nonnumeric, or noninteger; all available-MB samples negative or nonnumeric; and a missing, disabled, zero, negative, nonnumeric, noninteger, wildcard-only, or wrong-host policy. Translated names, multikv shape, duplicate-stanza cadence, and out-of-window events must fail the appropriate primary or source-health assertion. Test duplicate lookup rows separately: policy health must reject the deployment because a Splunk lookup can select one duplicate rather than safely proving uniqueness. When byte policy is met but `Pool Nonpaged Allocs` decreases after reboot, reset, or wrap, the primary row must remain and `allocation_calls_change` must be null.

dataSources: Primary source: local Windows Performance Data Helper counters collected by a custom `[perfmon://NonpagedPoolCritical]` input in the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), using `mode=single`, routed by convention to `index=perfmon sourcetype=Perfmon:Memory` every 60 seconds. Required `Memory` counters are `Pool Nonpaged Bytes` (current nonpaged-pool size in bytes; a last-observed gauge), `Pool Nonpaged Allocs` (number of calls to allocate nonpaged pool, regardless of bytes per call; context only), and `Available MBytes` (available physical memory in MB; context only). Required fields are `_time`, `host`, `object`, `counter`, and numeric `Value`; `useEnglishOnly=true` stabilizes exact names. The exact-host threshold comes from the governed `windows_nonpaged_pool_policy.csv` lookup, not from Windows telemetry.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for supported local Windows `perfmon://` collection and search-time knowledge. Deploy collection configuration to Windows Universal Forwarders or full Splunk Enterprise instances and add-on knowledge to the topology's required tiers. A Universal Forwarder runs the local input; it is not Splunkbase app 617 and does not itself provide the add-on.
spl:
index=perfmon sourcetype="Perfmon:Memory" object="Memory" counter IN ("Pool Nonpaged Bytes","Pool Nonpaged Allocs","Available MBytes") earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval numeric_value=tonumber(Value)
| eval nonpaged_bytes_sample=if(counter=="Pool Nonpaged Bytes" AND numeric_value>=0 AND numeric_value=floor(numeric_value),numeric_value,null()), nonpaged_allocs_sample=if(counter=="Pool Nonpaged Allocs" AND numeric_value>=0 AND numeric_value=floor(numeric_value),numeric_value,null()), available_mb_sample=if(counter=="Available MBytes" AND numeric_value>=0,numeric_value,null())
| bin _time span=5m
| stats avg(nonpaged_bytes_sample) as bucket_nonpaged_bytes latest(nonpaged_allocs_sample) as bucket_nonpaged_allocs avg(available_mb_sample) as bucket_available_mb count(nonpaged_bytes_sample) as byte_samples count(nonpaged_allocs_sample) as alloc_samples count(available_mb_sample) as available_samples by _time host
| where byte_samples>=4 AND alloc_samples>=4 AND available_samples>=4
| lookup windows_nonpaged_pool_policy host OUTPUT policy_id enabled critical_nonpaged_bytes policy_owner runbook
| eval enabled=tonumber(enabled), critical_nonpaged_bytes=tonumber(critical_nonpaged_bytes)
| where enabled=1 AND critical_nonpaged_bytes>0 AND critical_nonpaged_bytes=floor(critical_nonpaged_bytes) AND isnotnull(policy_id)
| eval qualifying_bucket=if(bucket_nonpaged_bytes>=critical_nonpaged_bytes,1,0)
| stats count as complete_buckets sum(qualifying_bucket) as qualifying_buckets min(_time) as observation_start max(_time) as last_bucket_start earliest(bucket_nonpaged_bytes) as first_nonpaged_bytes latest(bucket_nonpaged_bytes) as latest_nonpaged_bytes min(bucket_nonpaged_bytes) as minimum_nonpaged_bytes max(bucket_nonpaged_bytes) as peak_nonpaged_bytes min(bucket_available_mb) as lowest_available_mb earliest(bucket_nonpaged_allocs) as first_nonpaged_allocs latest(bucket_nonpaged_allocs) as latest_nonpaged_allocs by host policy_id critical_nonpaged_bytes policy_owner runbook
| where complete_buckets=3 AND qualifying_buckets=3
| eval observation_end=last_bucket_start+300, allocation_calls_change=if(latest_nonpaged_allocs>=first_nonpaged_allocs,latest_nonpaged_allocs-first_nonpaged_allocs,null()), first_nonpaged_gib=first_nonpaged_bytes/pow(1024,3), latest_nonpaged_gib=latest_nonpaged_bytes/pow(1024,3), minimum_nonpaged_gib=minimum_nonpaged_bytes/pow(1024,3), peak_nonpaged_gib=peak_nonpaged_bytes/pow(1024,3), critical_nonpaged_gib=critical_nonpaged_bytes/pow(1024,3)
| eval first_nonpaged_gib=round(first_nonpaged_gib,3), latest_nonpaged_gib=round(latest_nonpaged_gib,3), minimum_nonpaged_gib=round(minimum_nonpaged_gib,3), peak_nonpaged_gib=round(peak_nonpaged_gib,3), critical_nonpaged_gib=round(critical_nonpaged_gib,3), lowest_available_mb=round(lowest_available_mb,2), severity="critical", use_case="UC-1.2.23"
| table observation_start observation_end host severity policy_id policy_owner runbook complete_buckets qualifying_buckets critical_nonpaged_bytes critical_nonpaged_gib first_nonpaged_bytes first_nonpaged_gib latest_nonpaged_bytes latest_nonpaged_gib minimum_nonpaged_bytes minimum_nonpaged_gib peak_nonpaged_bytes peak_nonpaged_gib lowest_available_mb first_nonpaged_allocs latest_nonpaged_allocs allocation_calls_change use_case
| sort 0 -latest_nonpaged_gib host
description: Identifies sustained critical Windows nonpaged-pool consumption by requiring three complete five-minute buckets above an exact-host, reviewed byte boundary. It keeps physical-memory availability and cumulative allocation calls as separate context, validates counter completeness, and refuses to apply a universal 256 MB or RAM-percentage threshold. A result means the local critical policy was crossed; PoolMon or deeper tracing is still required for cause.
value: Nonpaged pool must remain resident in physical memory and supports kernel and driver work, so unchecked consumption can starve the operating system and destabilize every service on the host. A governed, persistent threshold gives Windows teams time to preserve tag-level evidence and coordinate a safe response before emergency reboot or broader availability impact, while avoiding obsolete one-size-fits-all limits that overpage large systems and miss smaller or specially constrained ones.
implementation: Install `Splunk_TA_windows`; deploy one `[perfmon://NonpagedPoolCritical]` event input for `Pool Nonpaged Bytes`, `Pool Nonpaged Allocs`, and `Available MBytes` with `mode=single`, `useEnglishOnly=true`, `interval=60`, and `index=perfmon`; then qualify units, field shape, cadence, duplicates, and native values. Create the exact-host `windows_nonpaged_pool_policy.csv` with one approved positive integer byte threshold per enabled host. Save the SPL as `windows_nonpaged_pool_critical_policy`, run it every five minutes, and retain three completed buckets after a five-minute delay. Use PoolMon or approved Windows Performance Toolkit/debugger procedures to identify tags and drivers; never infer them from host-level bytes.
visualization: Lead with source and policy health: expected hosts missing any counter, newest-event age, per-counter sample counts, duplicate-stanza indicators, hosts without exactly one enabled policy, and stale policy review dates. For qualified hosts, show separate 24-hour panels for `Pool Nonpaged Bytes` converted to GiB with the host's `critical_nonpaged_gib` line, `Available MBytes` in MB, and `Pool Nonpaged Allocs` as allocation calls; never combine their units or label allocation calls as outstanding objects. Add a ranked table matching the alert output, then drill down to raw counters, reboot/change annotations, PoolMon tag bytes/diff, driver inventory, and incident evidence. Show gaps as unknown and label findings as “critical policy exceeded,” not “confirmed leak” or “confirmed exhaustion.”
schema: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows Perfmon event fields plus Windows Memory performance-counter semantics; partial CIM Performance.Memory context
dataModelAcceleration: CIM Performance.Memory describes general host memory measures but does not preserve the Windows `Pool Nonpaged Bytes` gauge, `Pool Nonpaged Allocs`, exact raw counter identity, governed per-host byte threshold, three-counter sample completeness, or three-bucket persistence required here. Mapping nonpaged pool into generic `mem_used` would falsely equate one kernel pool with total used memory. No semantically equivalent `cimSpl` or accelerated `tstats` alert is claimed. A purpose-built summary is acceptable only if it retains every native unit, counter, host/time identity, sample count, bucket validity, and policy revision.

knownFalsePositives:
A result means the approved host policy was exceeded for 15 minutes. The measurement can be correct even when the cause is expected, bounded, or not a leak.

1. **Approved driver, storage, network, or failover stress test** — Kernel components can retain nonpaged allocations while a test raises I/O, connection, queue, or device concurrency. Confirm exact hosts, test owner, approved UTC bounds, expected peak bytes, PoolMon tags, and recovery criteria. Preserve the finding as control evidence and suppress only notification for the bounded interval.

2. **Boot, device discovery, or driver initialization** — Nonpaged usage can climb as Windows and drivers initialize devices, networking, filters, storage, security products, and virtualization integrations. Check boot time, driver/service start records, and whether the byte series reaches the approved post-boot plateau. A value that continues climbing after initialization remains actionable.

3. **Backup, antivirus, endpoint security, or filesystem filter workload** — Microsoft Defender, EDR, backup, encryption, deduplication, and storage filter drivers may legitimately hold nonpaged buffers during large scans or snapshots. Correlate job timing and PoolMon tag byte usage. Recovery after the job supports a bounded workload explanation; continuing tag growth does not.

4. **Network connection or packet-buffer surge** — A proxy, file server, firewall/filter driver, NIC driver, or connection-heavy service can increase kernel buffers under legitimate traffic. Compare connections, throughput, queue/dropped-packet counters, relevant pool tags, and service latency. Do not suppress solely because traffic is high when available memory or service health is degrading.

5. **Hyper-V, virtual-switch, storage, or device hot-add operation** — Live migration, dynamic memory, virtual-switch reconfiguration, storage attach, snapshot activity, and device changes can alter kernel pool demand. Correlate hypervisor and host change events. This use case measures the Windows instance on which collection runs and does not attribute guest versus host cause.

6. **Host-policy drift after RAM, OS, driver, or workload change** — A previously reviewed byte boundary can become too low or dangerously high after hardware resizing, Windows upgrade, driver replacement, registry override, or role change. Check policy review date and configuration inventory. Update the exact-host row through change control; do not add a permanent broad suppression.

7. **Large but stable, supported kernel workload** — Modern 64-bit Windows can legitimately use far more than 256 MB of nonpaged pool. A host may cross an obsolete or copied threshold without approaching its actual operational limit. This catalogue deliberately supplies no universal default; a bad policy row is governance failure, not proof that the counter is false.

8. **Allocation-call growth without byte growth** — `Pool Nonpaged Allocs` counts calls regardless of requested size and does not expose frees or current outstanding allocations. Rapid call growth can accompany normal churn, while a few large allocations can dominate bytes. Use the field only as context and use PoolMon's per-tag Allocs, Frees, Diff, and Bytes for diagnosis.

9. **Reboot, counter reset, or 32-bit raw-count wrap** — The allocation-call value can fall across reboot, reset, or wrap. The search sets `allocation_calls_change` to null rather than treating the decrease as negative allocation activity; byte thresholding is unaffected. Confirm boot identity and split diagnostics at the reset.

10. **Duplicate input or forwarding replay** — Two enabled Memory stanzas, deployment/local overlap, or replay can inflate sample counts and alter bucket averages. Compare 60-second cadence, `_indextime`, effective `btool` precedence, raw multiplicity, and forwarder identity. Repair collection rather than deduplicating measurements of uncertain provenance.

11. **Localized or alternate event shape** — Without `useEnglishOnly=true`, translated counters will not match. `PerfmonMk:Memory` multikv and `PerfmonMetrics:Memory` metric-index feeds do not automatically expose the documented scalar `counter`/`Value` contract. Missing results are source failure; qualify a separate normalization instead of broadening names by guesswork.

**Safe suppression:** leave the base measurement, policy, and source-health searches unchanged. Apply an approved time-bound exception only after the final result with the `windows_nonpaged_pool_exceptions.csv` lookup, keyed by exact `host` and `policy_id`, with numeric `valid_from_epoch`, exclusive `valid_until_epoch`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject wildcards, open-ended records, exceptions for missing telemetry, and exceptions that outlive the policy review. Retain suppressed results and expired-entry reviews.

The five-minute search scans a delayed 15-minute window, creates three buckets per host, and performs one exact-match lookup with no join, subsearch, transaction, or high-cardinality instance split.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and threshold contract

Assign a Windows platform owner, Splunk collection owner, search-content owner, driver/hardware escalation path, and change approver for host thresholds. Install a currently supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) on the Windows collection tier and make its parsing/search-time knowledge available where required. Use a Universal Forwarder or full Splunk Enterprise instance that can read local Windows performance counters and send to an approved event index. The search role needs that index, the governed lookup, and saved-search permissions. PoolMon, Windows Performance Recorder/Analyzer, kernel debugging, driver changes, and reboot privileges are diagnostic or remediation capabilities and must not be granted merely to run this read-only control.

`Memory\Pool Nonpaged Bytes` is a host-level **byte gauge**: current bytes allocated in the system nonpaged pool, whose pages must remain resident while allocated. It is not free bytes, a percentage, a rate, per-process nonpaged quota, or total kernel memory. Dividing it by 1,048,576 yields MiB and by `1024^3` yields GiB for display; the policy remains an integer byte value to avoid unit ambiguity.

There is no catalogue-wide safe or exhaustion threshold. Pool limits and practical headroom vary with architecture, Windows release, physical memory, kernel address-space policy, registry overrides, drivers, and workload. The former 256 MB rule reflects limits relevant to old Windows releases and is invalid as a universal modern rule. `Available MBytes` cannot serve as a nonpaged-pool denominator; it is broader available physical memory. Set `critical_nonpaged_bytes` per exact host from an approved baseline, supported Windows/hardware constraints, observed service impact, and a safe engineering margin. Record method, evidence, owner, and review date outside the minimal lookup if local governance requires those fields.

`Memory\Pool Nonpaged Allocs` is the number of calls to allocate nonpaged-pool space, regardless of bytes requested per call. It is not current outstanding allocations because this host-level counter does not supply matching frees; it is not pool capacity; and a rapid increase can represent normal small-allocation churn. The search retains first/latest values and calculates a change only when the counter does not decrease. A reset, reboot, or wrap yields null context and must not block a genuine byte-policy result.

The temporal contract uses three completed five-minute buckets from 20 minutes ago through five minutes ago. A 60-second input should provide about five observations per counter per bucket; at least four of all three are required. Every bucket must meet the same positive exact-host byte policy. The result therefore means 15 sustained minutes above policy after a five-minute indexing allowance. Missing counters, invalid values, missing policy, and policy duplication fail closed and must appear in independent health controls. Change the interval, four-sample minimum, delay, 15-minute persistence, or host threshold only with versioned tests.

## Step 1 — Configure the supported Memory counter input and policy

Do not edit `Splunk_TA_windows/default`. Deploy a version-controlled local stanza such as `%SPLUNK_HOME%\etc\apps\Splunk_TA_windows\local\inputs.conf`:

```ini
[perfmon://NonpagedPoolCritical]
disabled = 0
object = Memory
counters = Pool Nonpaged Bytes; Pool Nonpaged Allocs; Available MBytes
interval = 60
mode = single
useEnglishOnly = true
index = perfmon
sourcetype = Perfmon:Memory
```

The `Memory` object has no process/disk instance, so no `instances=*` setting is required. `mode=single` supplies one scalar `counter` and `Value` per event as assumed by the SPL. Keep this event-index contract separate from `PerfmonMk:Memory` multikv and `PerfmonMetrics:Memory` metric-index data. `useEnglishOnly=true` stabilizes the explicit English names; do not replace counters with wildcards.

Create `windows_nonpaged_pool_policy.csv` as an exact-match lookup with one and only one row per governed host:

```csv
host,policy_id,enabled,critical_nonpaged_bytes,policy_owner,runbook
win-pool-01,np-2026q3-01,1,4294967296,windows-platform,KB-WIN-NP-01
```

The example 4 GiB value is syntax only and must not be copied as a default. `host` must exactly match indexed metadata; `policy_id` must be nonempty and versioned; `enabled` is numeric 0 or 1; `critical_nonpaged_bytes` is a positive integer in bytes; owner and runbook are routing context. Reject wildcard hosts, duplicate host rows, locale-formatted numbers, unit suffixes, scientific notation, zero/negative values, and unreviewed inheritance from another host. Maintain a separate policy-health report for expected hosts without exactly one enabled current row and for rows whose inventory, Windows release, RAM, role, or review date has drifted.

Inspect canaries:

```powershell
& "$env:SPLUNK_HOME\bin\splunk.exe" btool inputs list perfmon://NonpagedPoolCritical --debug
Get-Counter '\Memory\Pool Nonpaged Bytes','\Memory\Pool Nonpaged Allocs','\Memory\Available MBytes' -SampleInterval 1 -MaxSamples 3
```

Confirm one winning stanza, the intended local app, enabled state, 60-second cadence, single mode, event index, source type, and exact names. Verify time synchronization, stable unique `host`, target-index access, output queues, and lookup visibility on the search head. At three events per minute, expect about 4,320 events per host per day. Measure actual bytes, latency, and forwarder/search cost before fleet rollout.

## Step 2 — Validate source values, units, policy, and health

Run at least a 30-minute qualification search:

```spl
index=perfmon sourcetype="Perfmon:Memory" object="Memory" counter IN ("Pool Nonpaged Bytes","Pool Nonpaged Allocs","Available MBytes") earliest=-30m
| eval numeric_value=tonumber(Value)
| stats count min(numeric_value) as minimum max(numeric_value) as maximum latest(_time) as newest by host counter
| eval age_seconds=now()-newest
| sort 0 host counter
```

Every expected host needs three rows, numeric nonnegative values, roughly 30 observations per counter, and a newest event within two intervals plus measured indexing delay. Nonpaged bytes and allocation calls should be integers; available MB can be represented numerically. Inspect raw events for scalar field shape and collection-time `_time`. Compare same-time values with Windows **Performance Monitor > Monitoring Tools > Performance Monitor** or `Get-Counter`. Task Manager's **Performance > Memory > Non-paged pool** can corroborate current scale, but a UI refresh is not authoritative for an exact historical sample. Small timing differences are expected; bytes versus displayed MiB/GiB must reconcile within display rounding.

Build source health independently. Report missing expected hosts; missing/stale counters; wrong object/index/source type; localized names; `PerfmonMk`/metric shape; nonnumeric or negative values; implausible fractional bytes/calls; call-counter reset/wrap; too few/many samples; duplicate input; replay; queue delay; host collision; and changed collection interval. Never `fillnull` a missing measurement with zero. A zero or low alert count cannot distinguish healthy pools from failed collection.

Build policy health independently. Enforce one exact row per expected host, unique nonempty `policy_id`, numeric `enabled`, positive integer bytes, approved owner/runbook, inventory match, revision/hash, review date, and no wildcard. The primary lookup returns one match but cannot itself prove that the backing CSV contains no duplicate host rows. Test lookup permissions from the scheduled-search owner. A host without policy must be a visible deployment gap; do not supply a hidden universal fallback.

## Step 3 — Create and understand the sustained policy alert

Save the catalogue SPL as `windows_nonpaged_pool_critical_policy`, schedule it every five minutes on a five-minute boundary, and trigger when result count is greater than zero. Keep `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m` in the SPL or apply equivalent dispatch bounds in saved-search configuration, not both. The latest five minutes are excluded for ingestion. Measure p95 delay and adjust only with tests and source-health coverage.

The base search selects the exact event-index, source-type, object, and three-counter contract. The first `eval` gives each counter a unit-specific field and converts `Value` numerically. `bin` creates three five-minute buckets. `stats` averages the byte and available-memory gauges, uses the latest allocation-call value, and counts each counter's samples. The validity gate requires four samples of each and nonnegative values.

The exact-host lookup supplies governance, not telemetry. Numeric conversion rejects malformed enabled/threshold values; missing policy IDs disappear from the alert and must be caught by policy health. Each complete bucket is compared with `>= critical_nonpaged_bytes`. The second aggregation requires exactly three complete and three qualifying buckets, keeps first/latest/minimum/peak bytes, lowest available MB, and allocation-call endpoints, and creates a null call delta after reset. GiB conversions are display fields only. No percentage of RAM, available memory, commit limit, or old 256 MB constant enters the decision.

A result means “this host exceeded its reviewed critical byte policy for 15 minutes,” not “Windows has exhausted the pool” and not “a driver leak is confirmed.” The title names the operational risk. Keep faster crash/event controls and longer-horizon trend reports alongside it. A slow leak below policy should appear on a separate baseline/slope report; a rapid exhaustion inside 15 minutes may require Windows events, service health, and a shorter host-specific emergency policy.

## Step 4 — Test arithmetic, governance failures, and native truth

Use absolute fixture times and an isolated event index. Load the positive scenario's 45 events: three counters, five one-minute observations, three buckets. Install only the exact test lookup row. Run a copy of the SPL with fixed bounds and assert one result, exact counts, threshold, first/latest bytes, GiB conversions, available MB, allocation endpoints, and observation end.

Run each negative independently. Boundary-test a bucket equal to the threshold (qualifies) and one byte below (does not). Test four versus three samples. Test missing/disabled/zero/negative/nonnumeric/wrong-host policy, and separately prove the policy-health control detects duplicate rows and wildcards. Test malformed telemetry, localized names, multikv shape, duplicated cadence, reset/wrap, reboot, and late/out-of-window events. When bytes qualify but allocation calls decrease, the primary alert should remain and `allocation_calls_change` should be null; do not let a context counter veto critical bytes.

On a representative Windows canary, compare indexed values with Performance Monitor, `Get-Counter`, and Task Manager during normal operation and a safe approved workload. Do not deliberately exhaust nonpaged pool, install a faulty driver, force a crash, or reboot a production host to test the alert. A synthetic fixture proves SPL logic; native comparison proves collection and units; neither validates a production critical threshold. Threshold acceptance requires Windows/hardware/workload owners and documented headroom evidence. Record exact bounds, versions, fixture and lookup hashes, expected/actual rows, alert delivery, native comparisons, policy approval, and exceptions. Keep `status=draft` until those runtime and governance checks are complete.

## Step 5 — Operationalize diagnosis, response, and evidence

Use the unit-separated dashboard in `visualization`, with source and policy health first. When a finding arrives, confirm three complete buckets, current telemetry, exact policy identity, no duplicate stanza, stable host identity, recent boot/driver/change context, and same-time native values. Check service latency, errors, available physical memory, commit, paged pool, paging, and kernel/system events without asserting a particular stop code.

Use PoolMon from an approved Windows Driver Kit/Debugging Tools installation to inspect nonpaged tags. Filter to nonpaged pool, sort by Bytes and by allocation-minus-free Diff, capture repeated timestamped snapshots, and use `/g` or the approved tag-to-driver mapping to identify likely components. PoolMon's per-tag Allocs/Frees/Diff/Bytes are different from the host-level `Pool Nonpaged Allocs` counter. A large tag is not automatically defective; look for sustained growth without corresponding frees and correlate with driver version and workload. Escalate to the vendor or driver owner. Use Windows Performance Recorder/Analyzer or kernel debugging only under expert procedure because tracing and debugging can add overhead or affect stability.

Do not automatically stop a driver, disable security/network/storage software, unload a filter, alter pool registry limits, capture a kernel dump, or reboot from this alert. Those actions can cause data loss, security gaps, network/storage outage, or destruction of diagnostic state. Preserve PoolMon and counter evidence first, verify the implicated component independently, follow the host/service runbook, obtain change approval, and coordinate recovery. After action, verify pool bytes fall below policy, available memory/service health recover, source data remains current, and the suspected tag no longer grows. Retain artifacts listed in `evidence`; the 30-day retention estimate is advisory.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot without false equivalence

- **No `Perfmon:Memory` events:** verify add-on assignment, `disabled=0`, effective `btool`, Windows service, index/routing, output queues, and role access. Inspect `splunkd.log` for `perfmon://NonpagedPoolCritical`; do not substitute process quota counters or WMI snapshots and claim the same contract.
- **Counter names are translated or missing:** confirm `useEnglishOnly=true`, explicit English text, and native availability through `Get-Counter -ListSet Memory` or `typeperf -qx`. Repair configuration rather than guessing aliases.
- **Events use `PerfmonMk:Memory`:** collection is multikv and does not satisfy scalar `counter`/`Value` assumptions. Restore `mode=single` or author and test separate extraction/cardinality logic.
- **Events use `PerfmonMetrics:Memory`:** metric indexes require verified metric names/dimensions and `mstats`. The event SPL is not interchangeable.
- **No result for a visibly high value:** check all three buckets, sample counts, five-minute delay, exact host lookup, enabled flag, integer byte unit, and policy ID. Do not inject a fallback threshold to make the alert fire.
- **Values appear 1,024 or 1,048,576 times wrong:** inspect raw `Value`; policy is bytes, `Available MBytes` is MB, and display uses binary GiB. Do not compare a GiB display number directly to byte policy.
- **Allocation calls decrease:** check reboot, uptime, counter reset/wrap, host collision, and raw order. Null delta is intentional. This context counter neither proves nor disproves a byte problem.
- **Available MB remains high:** possible; it is context, not pool capacity. Diagnose the approved byte threshold and tags rather than adding an undocumented available-memory gate.
- **Pool bytes are high but flat:** the critical policy can still be valid because it is a capacity rule, not a leak-only rule. Review workload, tag composition, service impact, and threshold approval. Use a separate slope control for leak suspicion.
- **Pool bytes rise but remain below policy:** retain the trend and investigate if sustained; this critical rule is intentionally silent. Do not call below-policy telemetry healthy when a longer-horizon control identifies growth.
- **CIM/tstats reports generic memory use instead:** expected. Generic `mem_used` is not nonpaged pool. Keep the raw counter contract or a governed summary preserving its semantics.
grandmaExplanation: We watch a part of Windows memory that the operating system and device drivers must keep in physical memory. If it stays above that computer's reviewed danger line, we warn the team so they can preserve clues and respond before the whole machine becomes unstable.
hardware: Windows physical servers, virtual machines, and supported Windows endpoints on which the local `perfmon://NonpagedPoolCritical` input executes. The counter describes the nonpaged pool of that Windows instance; it does not expose an underlying hypervisor's kernel pool, a remote WMI host, non-Windows kernels, container-specific limits, pool tags, or per-driver allocations.
